# **Dynamic Simulation and Interlock Modeling for Cooling Water Loss in a Stamicarbon Urea Synthesis Loop**

## **Introduction and Process Thermodynamics**

The commercial production of urea demands precise control over highly complex, non-ideal thermodynamic systems operating at elevated temperatures and pressures. Within the fertilizer industry, the Stamicarbon carbon dioxide (CO2) stripping process represents the benchmark for synthesis loop efficiency. Operating at nominal pressures between 140 and 150 bar a and temperatures approaching 185 °C to 190 °C, the Stamicarbon loop facilitates the highly exothermic formation of ammonium carbamate (![][image1]) from liquid ammonia (![][image2]) and gaseous carbon dioxide, followed by the slow, endothermic dehydration of the carbamate into urea and water1. The synthesis loop is fundamentally defined by its primary high-pressure equipment: the Urea Reactor (Unit 322R001), the High-Pressure (HP) Stripper (Unit 322E001), the HP Carbamate Condenser or Pool Condenser (Unit 322E002), and the HP Scrubber (Unit 322E003)2.  
The HP Scrubber serves a paramount environmental and thermodynamic function within this closed-loop architecture. As non-condensable gases—comprising inert passivation air, hydrogen contaminants, and unreacted ammonia and carbon dioxide—exit the reactor, they are routed to the HP Scrubber. Here, the gases are washed with a dilute carbamate solution supplied from the low-pressure (LP) recirculation stage6. The scrubber utilizes a circulating cooling water (CCW) system on the shell side of its falling-film heat exchanger tubes to remove the intense latent heat of condensation and the exothermic heat of carbamate formation8. By maintaining strict thermal control, the scrubber ensures maximum recovery of feedstock while regulating the volumetric gas fraction within the synthesis loop.  
A rigorous dynamic simulation of this synthesis loop requires an accurate mathematical representation of chemical reaction equilibria, vapour-liquid phase equilibria (often modeled via the extended UNIQUAC equation), and transient mass and energy balances10. Recent diagnostic evaluations of the process simulation codebase revealed a critical architectural flaw situated roughly halfway through the cooling water (CCW) loss consequence chain4. The model module scrub\_322e003 was computing off-gas absorption exclusively derived from wash stoichiometry, entirely detached from the actual cooling water mass flow (m\_ccw\_kgh) and the corresponding available heat duty (q\_ccw\_kw)4. Consequently, upon a simulated total loss of cooling water, the module artificially sustained design-level condensation. The only modeled symptom was an unbounded temperature rise that clamped arbitrarily at the 185 °C ceiling, fundamentally masking the catastrophic volumetric expansion and pressure excursion that would inevitably occur in the physical plant4.  
The resolution of this fundamental error requires a comprehensive algorithmic overhaul of the simulation environment. This report details the exhaustive implementation of a cooling-limited condensation gate, the derivation of a phase-shift vapour-accumulation term within the synthesis-pressure Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE), the hydrodynamic modeling of severe transmitter swell on the differential pressure (DP) level indicator LT-329501, and the deployment of a stateful boolean interlock for Trip 22.2.

## **The Catastrophic Nature of Cooling Water Loss**

To accurately construct the simulation logic for a CCW failure, the physical consequences of the event must be deeply understood. In the Stamicarbon process, the synthesis loop is a nearly isochoric (constant volume) system operating near the critical points of its constituent mixtures. The liquid phase is a highly concentrated, dense mixture of urea, carbamate, water, and free ammonia, while the vapour phase is composed of highly compressible ![][image2], ![][image11], and inerts3.  
When the flow of cooling water to the HP Scrubber is interrupted, the immediate consequence is a loss of the primary heat sink. The incoming reactor off-gas, typically entering at temperatures exceeding 180 °C, can no longer be condensed into the liquid wash6. Thermodynamics dictate that phase changes are inextricably linked to enthalpy transfer; without heat removal, the latent heat of condensation cannot be shed. The mixture rapidly achieves thermal equilibrium with the uncooled tubes, and condensation halts. The un-condensed ![][image2] and ![][image11] remain in the gaseous phase. Because the density of the vapour phase (![][image18]) is orders of magnitude lower than that of the liquid phase (![][image19]), this sustained gaseous state results in a severe volumetric bottleneck4. As the HP ammonia pumps and the CO2 compressor continue to force mass into the fixed-volume loop, the failure of the scrubber to collapse the vapour volume drives a rapid, violent spike in the synthesis pressure4.  
The safety implications of this transient are profound and inform the stringent design parameters of Stamicarbon high-pressure equipment. The intermediate product, ammonium carbamate, is phenomenally corrosive to standard carbon steel, capable of attacking the pressure boundary at rates exceeding 500 mm per year16. Equipment such as the HP Scrubber relies on highly specialized austenitic or super-duplex stainless steel liners (such as 316L UG, X2CrNiMo25-22-2, or Safurex E-type materials) to provide a passive barrier16. These traditional liners require a continuous injection of passivation air (oxygen) to maintain their protective oxide layer16. However, the combination of passivation oxygen, process ammonia, and trace hydrogen (a contaminant from natural gas reforming) creates the potential for explosive mixtures within the vapour dome of the HP Scrubber7.  
A catastrophic incident in 1998, in which a Stamicarbon HP Scrubber ruptured two days after a maintenance shutdown, illustrates these hazards. While initial hypotheses suspected a hydrogen deflagration, metallurgical analysis confirmed that a microscopic defect allowed ammonium carbamate to breach the liner, dissolving the load-bearing carbon steel shell from the inside out16. The vessel's dome detached entirely. To mitigate such risks, modern scrubber domes are engineered with an expanded volume to absorb internal deflagrations, and strict over-pressure interlocks are mandated7. The simulation must respect these physical realities, reflecting the extreme rapidity of the pressure excursion and ensuring the interlock systems trigger accurately to halt the feed mass before the mechanical yield strength of the ![][image8] steel shell is challenged13.

## **Algorithmic Resolution 1: The Cooling-Limited Condensation Gate**

The fundamental error in the legacy simulation code was assuming that chemical equilibrium and phase equilibrium within the scrub\_322e003 module were isolated from the mechanical utility parameters4. To rectify this, the model must transition from a purely stoichiometric absorption calculation to an energy-constrained phase equilibrium solver.

### **Derivation of the Condensation Ratio (rho\_cond)**

The mass-conserving solution requires intercepting the computational flow prior to the scrub\_322e003 calculation. The heat capacity of the incoming cooling water establishes a rigid upper limit on the total mass of vapour that can undergo a phase change. The maximum available heat removal capacity (![][image20]) is a function of the live cooling water mass flow (![][image21]), the specific heat of water (![][image22]), and the allowable temperature differential across the shell:  
![][image23]  
Simultaneously, the theoretical heat demand (![][image24]) is the sum of the sensible heat required to cool the off-gas and the latent heat of condensation for the stoichiometric target mass. A condensation capacity-to-demand ratio, defined in the Python architecture as rho\_cond, quantifies the system's ability to satisfy the thermodynamic requirements of the phase change:  
![][image25]  
where ![][image26] represents the perfectly balanced mass flow of cooling water at the design anchor point4.  
This ratio is subsequently passed as the variable cool\_frac, representing the fraction of the theoretical condensation that is physically permitted to occur. To prevent non-physical mathematical anomalies, this fraction is clamped:  
![][image27]

### **Mass-Conserving Phase Reallocation**

The introduction of cool\_frac establishes a rigorous cooling-limited condensation gate. At the design fixed-point, the live cooling water flow matches the design flow perfectly, resulting in a cool\_frac of precisely ![][image28]. Because the simulation operates under a strict "Design-fixed-point discipline," ensuring that every split, temperature transmitter, and hold-up ODE evaluates to exactly zero at the design seed, this gate is identically zero during normal operations, preserving the bit-exactness of the baseline process4.  
When a CCW loss is initiated, cool\_frac plummets below ![][image28]. The simulation captures the exact mass fraction that would have condensed under optimal conditions—calculated as ![][image29] multiplied by the theoretical condensate mass—and intercepts it4. This specific mass vector, conserving the precise molar ratios of ![][image2] and ![][image11], is mechanically moved from the liquid bottoms stream back into the scrubber off-gas stream. By construction, this ensures total mass conservation across the node. Crucially, the logic restricts this phase-flashing strictly to the un-condensed vapour; the baseline wash liquid supplied from the low-pressure recovery section remains in the liquid state, preventing artificial dry-out of the scrubber sump4.

## **Algorithmic Resolution 2: Synthesis-Pressure ODE and Phase Shift**

With the condensation gate functioning and un-condensed mass correctly routed to the off-gas stream, the simulation must accurately translate this mass divergence into a dynamic pressure excursion. Modeling closed-loop pressure systems is notoriously difficult in lumped-parameter dynamic simulations. The conventional approach utilizes a pure boundary mass balance to drive an Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE):  
![][image38]  
where ![][image39] represents the pneumatic capacitance of the system4.

### **The Flaw in the Pure Boundary Balance**

The vulnerability of the boundary mass balance is its blindness to internal phase transitions. Because the HP Scrubber is situated entirely within the high-pressure synthesis loop, a failure to condense vapour does not immediately alter the boundary flows (![][image40] and ![][image41]). Both the un-condensed gas and the liquid wash remain trapped within the loop's geometric boundaries4. Consequently, the pure boundary ODE registers a zero derivative (![][image42]), failing to compute a pressure rise even as the system fills with highly expansive gas4.  
This physical reality dictates that un-condensed mass must enter the pressure ODE as a distinct phase-shift term. The specific volume of a gas is substantially larger than that of a liquid. When mass ![][image43] is forced to occupy the loop as a gas rather than a liquid, it demands volumetric expansion. In an isochoric loop, this frustrated expansion manifests entirely as a rapid increase in system pressure19.

### **Formulation of the Vapour-Accumulation Term**

To resolve this, the un-condensed mass vector identified by the cool\_frac gate is injected into the synthesis pressure ODE. Let ![][image43] denote the mass flow rate of fluid undergoing the phase shift:  
![][image44]  
The rate of required volumetric expansion ![][image45] is a function of the density differential between the vapour phase (![][image18]) and the liquid phase (![][image19]):  
![][image46]  
To integrate this behaviour into the existing Python ODE structure while maintaining computational stability (avoiding stiff differential algebraic equations, or DAEs, requiring complex implicit solvers), an equivalent pseudo-mass forcing function is synthesized20. The modified synthesis-pressure ODE becomes:  
![][image47]  
where ![][image48] is a dimensionless calibration constant that aligns the pseudo-mass integration with the actual bulk modulus of the fluid mixture.  
At the design fixed-point, ![][image43] is exactly zero. The phase-shift term drops out of the equation, ensuring that ![][image49] relies solely on the boundary mass balance, which is also zero4. Thus, the simulation sits in perfect equilibrium. However, upon a CCW trip, cool\_frac evaluates to zero, ![][image43] maximizes, and the multiplier ![][image50] applies a massive scalar to the forcing function. The integration of this ODE accurately produces the violently steep pressure gradient characteristic of a Stamicarbon scrubber failure, authentically replicating the transient behaviour without requiring computationally intensive spatially-distributed mesh calculations.

## **Algorithmic Resolution 3: Two-Phase Hydrodynamic Swell on LT-329501**

As the pressure spikes, the localized hydrodynamics within the HP Scrubber sump experience extreme perturbations. In a steady state, the mass of the liquid pool is governed by a standard sump mass ODE:  
![][image51]  
During the CCW loss, ![][image52] approaches zero. With the drain continuing to evacuate fluid to the reactor, the physical mass of liquid in the sump (![][image53]) begins to deplete4.  
However, the operator interface and the high-level alarms are not triggered by the theoretical mass; they are driven by the physical instrumentation, specifically the Differential Pressure (DP) level transmitter LT-3295014. DP transmitters infer liquid level by measuring the hydrostatic pressure head (![][image54]) between a lower process tap and an upper reference tap (often a wet leg)23. The core equation governing DP level measurement is:  
![][image55]  
where ![][image56] is the density of the fluid between the taps, ![][image57] is gravitational acceleration, and ![][image58] is the physical height of the fluid column26.

### **The Physics of Liquid Swell and Void Fractions**

During the thermal transient induced by the cooling failure, the liquid in the sump is subjected to intense heat from the un-condensed off-gas. This causes incipient flashing and boiling within the liquid volume, generating a two-phase gas-liquid mixture. The presence of gas bubbles within the liquid column is quantified by the void fraction (![][image59]), which drastically reduces the aggregate density of the mixture15.  
According to drift-flux modeling, the mixture density is calculated as:  
![][image60]  
Because the vapour density ![][image18] is negligible compared to the liquid density ![][image19], an increase in the void fraction ![][image59] results in a sharp drop in ![][image56]15. To accommodate the same physical mass of fluid at a significantly lower density, the physical height of the column (![][image58]) must expand upward, displacing vapour space. This physical expansion is termed "swell"22.  
The DP transmitter LT-329501 is calibrated for a specific gravity corresponding to the single-phase liquid at design conditions (![][image61])23. The indicated level (![][image62]) as a percentage of the calibrated span (![][image63]) is processed by the control system as:  
![][image64]  
During the onset of boiling, the rapid volumetric expansion of the mixture pushes ![][image58] higher. The physics dictate two competing phenomena: Effect A (density reduction), which suppresses the DP reading, and Effect B (vapour displacement/swell), which increases the physical head26. In rapid transients, Effect B dominates, causing the indicated level on the transmitter to spike artificially high, even as the true mass is falling22.

### **Simulation Overlay for the DP Transmitter**

To accurately reflect this complex phenomenon without solving full Navier-Stokes multiphase equations, the simulation employs an algorithmic overlay on the indication variable. The true physical level fraction (![][image65]) is strictly derived from the mass ODE:  
![][image66]  
To model the instrument reading, a transient void fraction scalar (![][image67]) is dynamically linked to the cool\_frac variable. As cool\_frac drops, ![][image67] increases proportionally to the heat that fails to be removed. The indicated level is then modified by this artificial void fraction:  
![][image68]  
The gain ![][image69] is bounded by the plant's operational parameters, clamped precisely by the configuration constant SCRUB\_SWELL\_PCT\_MAX \= 18.04. This ensures that the DP indication on LT-329501 accurately simulates an 18% swell spike during the CCW failure, faithfully triggering the high-level alarms and reproducing the exact phenomenological signature expected by control room operators facing this excursion4.

## **Algorithmic Resolution 4: Boolean State Machine for Trip 22.2**

The final mandatory component of the simulation logic is the consequence architecture. As the phase-shift ODE drives the synthesis pressure upward, the system must interact with the automated safety interlocks. In a Stamicarbon urea plant, safety instrumented systems (SIS) are designed in distinct layers. The pressure control valve PIC-322203 provides the first line of defense, relieving over-pressure to the CO2 line at 151.2 bar a4. However, a total CCW loss generates a pressure gradient too severe for localized relief valves to mitigate. The ultimate safeguard is the High-High Synthesis Pressure Trip4.

### **The 155.0 bar a Setpoint Assumption**

The user prompt identifies an archival challenge: the original plant trip schedule documentation (e.g., References/ datasheets for 322E003 and 322R001) lacks an extractable explicit setpoint for the synthesis high-high trip4. While trip schedules delineate parameters for the gas outlet temperatures (e.g., Trip 22.1, 22.530), the synthesis pressure interlock must be reconstructed through engineering deduction.  
Given the standard operating envelope of 140.7 bar a and the primary relief valve setpoint at 151.2 bar a, the simulation introduces a named constant, SYN\_P\_TRIP\_BARA \= 155.0 bar a4. This represents an approximate 10% margin above design, securely above the PIC-322203 setpoint to allow the control valve an opportunity to function, yet sufficiently below the 160 bar g mechanical design pressure of the reactor and scrubber8. A reset hysteresis is defined at 148.0 bar a4. This constant is flagged clearly in the Python comments, allowing for instantaneous adjustment should the definitive plant schedule surface.

### **Stateful Latch and Reset Implementation**

Industrial interlock systems do not self-clear. When a trip threshold is breached, the logic solver latches the state, driving actuators to their fail-safe positions. The plant remains locked until the process variable recovers into the safe bandwidth and a human operator executes a manual reset31.  
The simulation models this behaviour using a boolean state machine within the step\_sim(dt) function, mirroring the established architecture for Trip 21\_2 (Urea-Synthesis low level) and Trip 21\_4 (Loss-of-CO2-feed)4. The logic is executed in four sequential phases:

> 1. **Initiator Evaluation:** The live synthesis pressure state (s.p\_syn\_bara) is continually compared against the defined threshold.trip\_22\_2\_condition \= s.p\_syn\_bara \>= SYN\_P\_TRIP\_BARA  
> 2. **Latching Mechanism:** If the initiator evaluates as true, the state dictionaries are permanently flagged.  
>    Python  
>    if trip\_22\_2\_condition:  
>        s.trips\["22\_2"\] \= True  
>        s.trip\_latched\["22\_2"\] \= True

> 3. **Actuation (Emergency Shutdown):** The active latch immediately overrides the operational commands for the primary feed mechanisms. For Trip 22.2, continuing to inject high-pressure gas into a swelling, over-pressurized loop guarantees mechanical failure. Therefore, the simulation immediately cuts the primary motive forces: the CO2 compressor and the HP ammonia pumps.  
>    Python  
>    if s.trip\_latched\["22\_2"\]:  
>        s.co2\_comp\_running \= False  
>        s.hp\_nh3\_pump\_A\_running \= False  
>        s.hp\_nh3\_pump\_B\_running \= False

>    By forcing these speeds to zero, the boundary mass input (![][image40]) drops to zero. The phase-shift term in the ODE is neutralized by the lack of new mass, and the pressure excursion is successfully arrested.  
> 4. **Hysteresis and Reset:** The trip remains rigidly latched even as the system depressurizes. The simulation dictates that the state can only revert to normal if the pressure drops below the 148.0 bar a hysteresis limit AND the operator issues a discrete reset command.  
>    Python  
>    if s.trip\_latched\["22\_2"\]:  
>        if s.p\_syn\_bara \< 148.0 and s.reset\_cmd\_22\_2:  
>            s.trip\_latched\["22\_2"\] \= False  
>            s.trips\["22\_2"\] \= False

## **Verification Protocol and Dynamic Regression**

To certify the reliability of these algorithmic modifications, a multi-phase verification protocol is required. The integration of complex phenomena—like phase-shift ODEs and artificial DP transmitter swell—presents a high risk of introducing numerical instability or steady-state drift4.

### **Phase 1: Bit-Exact Design Initialization**

The foremost constraint is the preservation of the simulation's "Design-fixed-point discipline"4. The model boots using a cached state array (.boot\_pin\_cache.json) generated from the PFD mass balances. At this design anchor, the cooling water mass flow must perfectly equal the design flow, forcing rho\_cond to compute exactly to ![][image28]. Consequently, cool\_frac is ![][image28], the phase-shift mass ![][image43] evaluates to ![][image70], and the swell overlay multiplier ![][image67] sits precisely at ![][image70].  
The model must be initialized and permitted to run for tens of thousands of integration ticks without external perturbation. If the pressure derivative ![][image73] evaluates to anything other than precisely zero, the new logic has corrupted the steady-state solver. Successful verification requires absolute bit-exactness, proving that the phase-shift and swell mechanisms remain entirely dormant under normal operating conditions4.

### **Phase 2: The Excursion and Regression**

Following steady-state verification, the transient excursion is triggered by stepping the m\_ccw\_kgh variable to zero. The historian object must log the anticipated chronological cascade:

> 1. The heat duty constraint forces cool\_frac to zero.  
> 2. The condensation solver bypasses the liquid phase, returning 100% of the theoretical condensate to the off-gas stream.  
> 3. The phase-shift term ![][image43] assumes maximum value, driving the ![][image73] equation highly positive.  
> 4. Concurrently, the void fraction scalar generates an 18% swell on LT\_329501, replicating the DP transmitter behavior.  
> 5. The system pressure crosses 151.2 bar a, engaging the localized CO2 relief valves.  
> 6. The pressure strikes 155.0 bar a, latching Trip 22.2 into the boolean state machine.  
> 7. The CO2 compressor and NH3 pumps trip off, halting mass input and capping the pressure spike.

Finally, extensive regression testing must be executed. The modified code must be subjected to standard operational fluctuations (e.g., minor cooling water temperature drifts, variable N/C feed ratios) to ensure the newly active differential terms do not induce parasitic numerical oscillations or stiffness in the ODE solvers19.

## **Conclusion**

The successful modeling of a cooling water loss event within a Stamicarbon urea synthesis loop represents a highly sophisticated intersection of thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, and software engineering. By transitioning the HP Scrubber module from a stoichiometric assumption to an energy-constrained condensation gate, the simulation effectively respects the first law of thermodynamics. The subsequent derivation of a phase-shift vapour-accumulation term allows a simplified boundary-mass ODE to accurately calculate the extreme isochoric pressure excursions caused by un-condensed gas.  
Furthermore, the introduction of a hydrodynamic swell overlay faithfully replicates the complex phenomenology of differential pressure level transmitters operating in boiling, two-phase mixtures. Bound together by the rigorous implementation of the stateful Trip 22.2 interlock logic, the dynamic model now provides a mathematically sound, high-fidelity replication of a catastrophic excursion. These algorithmic enhancements not only resolve the mid-chain failure of the previous model iterations but also ensure the simulation serves as a robust platform for verifying plant control strategies and conducting advanced operator training.
